5.	For 27 years, two neighboring countries were locked in one of the world's most peculiar diplomatic standoffs — a quarrel not over territory, or resources, or ideology, but over a name. When the smaller country declared independence in 1991 after the breakup of Y, it adopted the name X of a region that its larger neighbor considered part of its own ancient heritage. The larger country argued that the name implied territorial claims on its own northern province and blocked the X's entry into NATO and the EU for nearly three decades. At the UN, the X was forced to use the awkward provisional designation "the Former Y Republic of X." The deadlock was finally broken in 2018 when the two prime ministers signed an agreement on the shores of Lake Prespa. X agreed to add the directional modifier Z to its name making it “Z X,” and the deal opened the door to NATO membership.
